title: Conscience
hook: the inner voice, formed by prayer and learning, to be followed

segments.voice: Yesterday, works of mercy for the soul: Job's friends, silent and then too sure. Your line was mercy with words. Which word of mercy did you speak? Day one thousand two hundred ten.

A cave in the wilderness. In the dark at the back, David and his men are hiding from King Saul, who has come with an army to kill him. And then Saul himself walks into the very same cave, alone, and has no idea who is in there with him. David's men whisper: this is the day. God has handed him to you. David creeps forward in the dark and quietly cuts a corner off the king's robe. That's all. Then he goes back. And the King James text says: "David's heart smote him, because he had cut off Saul's skirt." Not for killing him. For a piece of cloth. Today: conscience.

Something in David spoke up, and it spoke up over something small. His men saw a chance. His conscience saw the king. David tells his men he will not lift his hand against "the LORD's anointed," and his heart struck him for even the corner of the robe. He listens, and he holds his men back. Christians call that inner voice conscience, and Paul writes about it. Writing to the Romans, he describes people who never had the law of Moses but still know right from wrong, the work of the law "written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness." A witness inside, testifying. Sometimes accusing, sometimes excusing. Then comes a caution. Christian teaching says conscience has to be formed. It isn't automatically right. A conscience can be dulled by habit, or made too harsh, or trained by a crowd. Paul spends whole chapters on believers whose consciences disagree about what's allowed, and he asks them to be patient with each other. So Christians tend a conscience the way you tend a garden: with prayer, with scripture, with the teaching of their church, with honest friends. A psalm puts the prayer side of it simply: "Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts." And then, once it's formed, conscience is to be followed. Paul tells a Roman governor, in Acts, that he works "to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men." Churches speak of this in their own ways. Catholic teaching calls conscience a judgment a person must obey, and must also form. Some Protestant teachers speak of a conscience bound to scripture. In both, it's the place where a person stands alone before God.

Here's the practice: listen to your conscience once. Settle, and breathe. Let the last day or two pass slowly through your mind. A conversation. An email. A choice. Somewhere in there, see if there's a small place where something tugged, the way David's heart smote him over a corner of cloth. Don't argue with it yet, and don't punish yourself. Just listen to what it's saying. If you pray, you can borrow the psalm: search me, O God, and know my heart. The bell holds the time.
Conscience. The inner witness that knows right from wrong, formed by prayer and learning, and then followed.
Your line: the inner voice. Today, when something small tugs at you, a corner of cloth, stop long enough to hear it, and then do what it asks. Day one thousand two hundred ten.

howItsDone: Christians form conscience through prayer, scripture, the teaching of their church and the counsel of others, and some examine their conscience at the end of the day or before confession or communion.

original.note: Greek: conscience, an inner knowing. Paul's word in Romans 2:15 and Acts 24:16.

trapdoor: what you thought: conscience is a feeling of guilt.
what it means: the inner witness to right and wrong, which Christians form with prayer and learning, and then follow.
what a scholar hears: Paul's syneidesis in Romans 2:15, a witness that accuses or excuses, and his patience with differing consciences.

notes: Hook follows 1 Samuel 24:1–7 (cave of En-gedi; Saul enters; David's men urge him; David cuts the skirt of the robe; his heart smites him; he restrains his men). 'With a knife' is implied, not stated; confirm or cut.
Romans 2:14–15 speaks of Gentiles without the law; the script paraphrases it as 'people who never had the law of Moses'. Confirm.
Acts 24:16 is addressed to the governor Felix; confirm 'a Roman governor'.

Church summaries: Catholic teaching (conscience as a judgment of reason to be obeyed and formed); 'some Protestant teachers speak of a conscience bound to scripture' (echoing Luther at Worms, not quoted). Confirm fairness.
howItsDone says 'some examine their conscience' (daily examen, examination before confession or communion). Confirm.
Original: συνείδησις; 'an inner knowing' avoids the 'knowing-with' etymology. Confirm.

Editor pass: 'with a knife' cut (1 Samuel 24:4 names no blade); stock 'here's the part that keeps it honest' replaced. Keeper note: David is the hook figure on days 1202, 1207 and 1210, and Saul hunting David also appears on 1202; the cave is kept because 'David's heart smote him' is the clearest conscience text, but a different hook could be swapped in.
Audit (2026-10-02): teach now gives the text's own reason for David's restraint, 'the LORD's anointed' (1 Samuel 24:6), instead of the vaguer 'a man he would not harm'.
